matching.reasoningTemplate: Episodic breathlessness and wheeze without fever or consolidation suggests bronchospasm.

clinicalPearls: An exacerbation is an episode of acute bronchospasm that may be severe enough to require emergency care or hospitalization and can be fatal (p.2216).
During an acute attack patients typically show tachypnea, tachycardia and accessory-muscle use, with wheezing and a prolonged expiratory phase (p.2222).
As airway obstruction worsens the chest may become 'silent' with loss of breath sounds, indicating a more dangerous attack rather than improvement (p.2222).
Most patients in an attack are hypocapnic from a high respiratory rate; a normal or near-normal PaCO2 in a distressed asthmatic signals impending respiratory failure (p.2227).
PEFR, FEV1 and FEV1/FVC are reduced in obstruction, but these may appear normal during an attack or after recent bronchodilator use, so a normal value does not exclude severe disease (p.2222-2223).

In urgent care, PEFR/FEV1 should be measured; patients with PEFR >60% predicted often respond to beta2-agonists alone, whereas failure to reach >60% or persistent severe tachypnea over 4-6 h should prompt hospital admission (p.2227).
Severe exacerbations requiring systemic corticosteroids may themselves accelerate long-term lung-function decline (p.2221).
More than one-third of patients carrying a physician diagnosis of asthma do not actually meet diagnostic criteria, so consider mimics when an 'asthmatic' fails to respond (p.2222).
Some patients cannot distinguish an anxiety attack from an asthma attack, which can confound assessment of an apparent exacerbation (p.2222).
harrison.pathophysiology: Asthma is characterized by episodic, usually reversible airway obstruction with airway hyperresponsiveness, generally accompanied by airway inflammation (most often eosinophilic, sometimes neutrophilic, occasionally with no obvious inflammation). Exacerbations are episodes of acute bronchospasm driven by luminal narrowing from airway smooth-muscle constriction, airway edema and mucus secretion, superimposed on chronic airway inflammation. Triggers activate mast cells/basophils and inflammatory cells (releasing bronchoconstrictors and mediators) and stimulate sensory nerves acting on smooth muscle. Allergen exposure can cause an immediate (early) bronchospasm and a late response 2-24 h later with airway narrowing and inflammation. Structural airway-wall thickening (smooth-muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia, subepithelial collagen deposition, edema, mucosal inflammation) increases the tendency to narrow disproportionately. In severe airflow obstruction there may be air trapping with dynamically elevated FRC and increased residual volume; mild hypoxemia from ventilation-perfusion mismatch (oxygen-responsive) is common (p.2216-2217, p.2221, p.2222-2223).
additionalDifferentials: Heart failure (overlapping symptoms; can produce obstructive pulmonary function) (p.2222)
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / asthma-COPD overlap (p.2222, p.2228)
Airway obstruction from a mass or foreign body (p.2222)
Anxiety attacks (may be indistinguishable from an asthma attack) (p.2222)
nonInfectiousMimics: Inducible laryngeal obstruction (vocal-cord dysfunction): inappropriate laryngeal narrowing causing airflow resistance; more common in women and in those with anxiety/depression; can both mimic and complicate asthma; diagnosed by laryngoscopy during symptoms (p.2222)
Heart failure / left ventricular dysfunction as a cause of dyspnea and obstructive-pattern symptoms (p.2222)
Anaphylaxis as a cause of acute generalized bronchospasm (p.2222 differential; mechanism noted elsewhere in text)
additionalInvestigations: Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) and FEV1 to quantify obstruction and guide disposition; PEFR >60% predicted predicts response to beta2-agonists alone (p.2222-2223, p.2227)
Arterial blood gas / PaCO2 monitoring: hypocapnia is usual, while a normalizing or rising PaCO2 indicates impending respiratory failure (p.2227)
Pulse oximetry / assessment of hypoxemia (V/Q mismatch, oxygen-responsive) (p.2216-2217, p.2227)
Bronchodilator reversibility testing (>=10-12% FEV1 improvement) when not in an acute attack (p.2222-2223)
Methacholine, mannitol or exercise/cold-air challenge to demonstrate airway hyperresponsiveness when PFTs are non-confirmatory (not during an acute attack) (p.2223)
Blood eosinophil count (correlates with severity; very high levels prompt consideration of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis) (p.2223)
Total/specific IgE, skin or RAST testing; IgE >1000 IU/mL prompts consideration of ABPA (p.2223)
Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) as a marker of type 2 inflammation and ICS adherence (p.2223)
Chest CT in poorly responsive disease to assess bronchiectasis/structural causes; sinus imaging and serum alpha-1 antitrypsin in selected cases (p.2223)
redFlags: Silent chest with loss of breath sounds (life-threatening) (p.2222)
Normal or near-normal PaCO2 in a distressed asthmatic, or a rising PaCO2 - signals impending respiratory failure and possible need for mechanical ventilation (p.2227)
Respiratory exhaustion / failure to respond to repeated beta2-agonists (p.2227)
Failure to achieve PEFR >60% predicted or persistent severe tachypnea over 4-6 h (warrants admission) (p.2227)
Need for hourly beta2-agonists for several hours despite treatment (p.2227)
Status asthmaticus: severe attack in which mechanical ventilation is difficult due to high airway resistance/pressures (p.2227)
harrison.prognosis: Asthma causes significant morbidity and mortality; roughly 3000-4000 people die from asthma each year in the United States. Death can occur even in mild asthma (at lower rates than severe asthma). Mortality in patients over 65 is about five times that of younger cohorts. High-risk features for asthma death include prior ICU admission or intubation for asthma, illicit drug use, depression, a new diagnosis within the past year, two or more emergency visits in the past 6 months, severe psychosocial problems, lower socioeconomic status, and being on daily prednisone before admission. Severe exacerbations may accelerate long-term lung-function decline (p.2221, p.2227).
pitfalls: Interpreting a 'silent chest' or quieting wheeze as improvement when it actually signals worsening, life-threatening obstruction (p.2222).
Being reassured by a normal/normalizing PaCO2 - in a distressed asthmatic this is an ominous sign of impending respiratory failure, not stability (p.2227).
Relying on PFT/PEF values that may look normal during an attack or shortly after bronchodilator use (p.2222-2223).
Overlooking mimics such as vocal-cord dysfunction, heart failure or COPD in 'difficult' or treatment-refractory presentations - over one-third of diagnosed asthmatics do not meet criteria (p.2222).
Missing precipitants such as beta-blockers (including ophthalmic drops), aspirin/NSAIDs in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, or ACE-inhibitor cough (p.2221).
Giving antibiotics routinely in an exacerbation - they should be used only if there are signs of infection (p.2227).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison stratifies acute deteriorations practically rather than by a fixed table. Mild-to-moderate deteriorations can initially be managed with frequent beta2-agonists; failure to control with hourly beta2-agonists for several hours warrants urgent care. In urgent/ED care, PEFR or FEV1 guides severity: PEFR >60% predicted usually responds to beta2-agonists alone, whereas failure to reach PEFR >60% or persistent severe tachypnea over 4-6 h indicates a severe attack needing admission. Life-threatening / near-fatal features include silent chest, respiratory exhaustion, and a normal or rising PaCO2 signaling impending respiratory failure; status asthmaticus denotes a severe refractory attack with high airway resistance making ventilation difficult (p.2227).
